title: Artificial intelligence: AI giant offers compute use in national interest
full_text:
Anthropic is open to reserving a portion of its computing power for government priorities such as healthcare as part of its efforts to win community support to operate in Australia.
Jeff Bleich, Washington's former ambassador in Australia and now an international envoy at Anthropic, acknowledged a letter written by the Labor-chaired, bipartisan parliamentary inquiry into artificial intelligence which urged the federal government to invest in data centres and recommended that computing capacity be reserved for the national interest.
He said the government was not going to "chip in" on the building of future data centres. Rather, as part of establishing trust, Anthropic was open to negotiating to set aside a "certain amount of compute", "within bounds". A mechanism for securing capacity wasn't put forward by the inquiry.
The developer of the Claude platform signed a deal to build the country's single largest data centre, north-west of Brisbane, last month.
"We'd be open to that sort of proposal because at the end of the day, we're bringing a lot of compute to the country," Bleich said. "We want the country to be successful. We want the economic prosperity and the national security that comes with this technology to be shared with our partners on the frontier, and that means that if there are things that are going to make Australia stronger, healthier, safer and more prosperous, we can be part of that solution with the government."
Asked how Anthropic would respond to the Australian government insisting on independent assessors being given early access to its AI models - another request in the letter - Bleich said he welcomed oversight.
"We're big on having independent assessors evaluate our work," he said, referencing Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei's call to embed external evaluators in frontier models as part of a push to slow down development.
"With Mythos, we didn't release it to the public, even though [we had] a highly valuable product. We wanted to make sure that it was going to be safe and responsibly deployed, so we worked with close partners, including here in Australia, so they could identify their vulnerabilities and patch them and make themselves more secure.
"We brought them into the tent on the technology. We'd be happy to continue to do that kind of work, as well as work with the Australian AI Safety Institute," he told the summit.
Mythos, Anthropic's large language model that is adept at identifying and exploiting vulnerabilities in major operating systems and web browsers, was previewed in April but not publicly released due to fears it could put the entire global financial system at risk. A handful of large US companies were granted access to assess the model's capabilities under Project Glasswing.
The letter isn't the first time the federal government has zeroed in on compute capacity. Assistant Technology Minister Andrew Charlton flagged in August that the government was considering forcing AI giants to make data centre capacity available to local start-ups and innovators. He argued that compute had become as essential to research and innovation as laboratories and libraries.
Anthropic first revealed its plans to come to Australia in July, pitching to buy at least 1.4 gigawatts of capacity. It's since committed to building a centre at Queensland's Western Downs Digital Park. The company will use its data centre for inference - answering prompts and directing agents to act. Copyright law prevents Anthropic from training its AI models on shore. Amendments are being considered.
Bleich said no state was "out of contention" for the building of future data centres. "We've literally had a number of projects brought to us," he said. Anthropic wants its data centres to be run on renewable energy, but Bleich said gas "could" be considered. Its centres use little to no water.
